stories.bridge: Now that you know where the bit came from, let's count information — starting with the mathematics of how much a message can surprise you.

figures.name: Claude Shannon
figures.role: Founder of information theory; MIT master's thesis 1937

stories.hook: In 1936, a 20-year-old named Claude Shannon arrived at MIT — carrying two ideas that would become your phone.
stories.narrative: Shannon had grown up in Gaylord, Michigan, building radios and telegraphs from scrap, and he arrived at MIT with a rare double gift: he thought like an engineer and like a mathematician at once. At twenty, working with the differential analyzer — a room-sized mechanical computer — he wrote his master's thesis, 'A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits,' submitted in 1937 and published in 1938. Its claim was breathtaking in hindsight: George Boole's century-old algebra of true and false was the perfect mathematics for designing electrical circuits. Switches in series were AND; switches in parallel were OR. Logic became hardware. The thesis has been called the most important master's thesis ever written, and it more or less founded digital circuit design. Then Shannon went to Bell Labs, and during the war years he thought about a deeper question: what is information, mathematically? The answer came in 1948, in 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication,' published in the Bell System Technical Journal: information is the resolution of uncertainty, measured in binary digits — bits. The entropy formula, the channel capacity theorem, the noisy-channel coding theorem: the entire science of moving bits reliably through an unreliable world, in one paper. Here's the line the reel got right: your phone runs on both ideas. The Boolean circuits switch the bits; the information theory squeezes them through the air. Two ideas, one twenty-year-old, twelve years apart. When you count information in this module — when you compute how many bits a message carries — you're doing 1948. Shannon gave you the unit. That same paper also gave us the noisy-channel coding theorem — the proof that reliable communication over unreliable channels is possible at any rate below capacity — which is why your phone works in a tunnel. Two papers, twelve years apart, one twenty-year-old's intuition compounded: first make logic physical, then make information measurable. Count carefully in this module; the bit is watching.
stories.title: The story behind the bit
verifiedClaims: Shannon's MIT master's thesis was submitted in 1937 and published in 1938
'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' was published in the Bell System Technical Journal in 1948
The thesis applied Boolean algebra to relay and switching circuits

stories.bridge: Boole mathematized thought; Shannon electrified it. Now let's learn the algebra itself — the logic underneath every proof you'll write.
stories.hook: In 1847, George Boole — a self-taught schoolteacher's son — published the mathematics of thought.
stories.narrative: Boole never attended university. The son of a cobbler in Lincoln, England, he taught himself mathematics from borrowed books while working as a schoolteacher, and by his twenties he was publishing original work. In 1847 he released a slim pamphlet, 'The Mathematical Analysis of Logic,' with an audacious thesis: the laws of human reasoning could be expressed as algebra. Let x and y stand for classes of things; let multiplication be intersection, addition be union; then reasoning becomes calculation. He expanded it in 1854 into 'An Investigation of the Laws of Thought,' one of the founding texts of mathematical logic. The world mostly shrugged. For seventy years Boolean algebra was a curiosity, admired by logicians and used by almost no one — until 1937, when a 20-year-old named Shannon showed it was the mathematics of electrical switches, and suddenly Boole's abstraction was the blueprint for every digital circuit on Earth. Boole died in 1864 at 49, after walking through the rain to lecture and catching pneumonia; he never knew. The pattern is worth noticing: the most practical mathematics often begins as the most abstract. Boole wasn't trying to build computers — they didn't exist. He was trying to understand thought. The engineers came later, and found his tools waiting. In this module you'll learn Boolean algebra as pure logic: sets, operations, proofs. Learn it the way Boole meant it — as the structure of reasoning — and the circuits will take care of themselves. Boole's work fed directly into the logicism of Frege and Russell — the attempt to ground all mathematics in logic — and his daughter Mary Everest Boole became a noted mathematics educator. The algebra waited seventy years for its application, then became the most-applied mathematics in history. In this module you'll meet Boolean algebra as pure structure; remember that the purest structures find the widest uses, usually decades later.
stories.title: The story behind Boolean algebra
verifiedClaims: Boole published 'The Mathematical Analysis of Logic' in 1847 and 'The Laws of Thought' in 1854
He was self-taught, never attended university
Shannon applied Boolean algebra to circuits in his 1937 thesis

stories.bridge: Newton and Leibniz gave you the machinery; three centuries of mathematicians made it rigorous. Now let's learn to differentiate — the mathematics of change itself.

figures.name: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz
figures.role: Published the first calculus paper, 1684; created the modern notation

stories.hook: In 1665, plague closed Cambridge — so Isaac Newton went home to the family farm and invented calculus.
stories.narrative: Newton was 22 when the Great Plague shut the university. In eighteen months of rural isolation — his annus mirabilis, the miraculous year — he developed the method of fluxions (his calculus), the theory of gravitation, and the fundamentals of optics. He told almost no one, and published almost nothing; the calculus circulated privately for decades. Meanwhile, in Germany, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz — philosopher, diplomat, polymath — independently developed his own version and, crucially, published first: 'Nova Methodus' in the Acta Eruditorum in 1684, with the notation we still use — dy/dx, the integral sign ∫, the whole elegant machinery. What followed was the ugliest priority dispute in scientific history. Newton's allies accused Leibniz of plagiarism; the Royal Society's 1712 investigation, secretly written by Newton himself as Society president, found in Newton's favor. The feud split European mathematics for a century — and ironically, Britain lost, clinging to Newton's dot notation while the continent computed happily in Leibniz's superior symbols. The foundations were shaky too: in 1734, Bishop Berkeley mocked infinitesimals as 'the ghosts of departed quantities,' and it took Cauchy and Weierstrass in the 19th century to make limits rigorous. But the machinery worked, and it worked on everything: motion, heat, electromagnetism, economics. When you take a derivative in this module, use Leibniz's notation and remember the farm in 1665 — the most productive quarantine in history. The priority war's collateral damage was real: British mathematics, loyal to Newton's fluxions, fell behind the continent for a century — a cautionary tale about letting nationalism steer notation. Rigor arrived in the 1800s when Cauchy and Weierstrass rebuilt calculus on limits, answering Berkeley's ghosts at last. What you learn in this module is their cleaned-up version: the farm boy's insight, the diplomat's notation, the analysts' rigor, compounded. Learn the rigor; honor the farm.
stories.title: The story behind calculus
verifiedClaims: Newton developed calculus during his 1665–1666 isolation
Leibniz published 'Nova Methodus' in 1684 with the modern notation
The Royal Society's 1712 report on the priority dispute was authored by Newton himself

stories.bridge: The bell curve is where probability meets the real world. Now let's learn the distributions — and why so many of them are secretly normal.

figures.name: Abraham de Moivre
figures.role: First derived the normal curve as a limit (1738)

figures.name: Carl Friedrich Gauss
figures.role: Developed the normal distribution for astronomical errors (1809)

figures.name: Adolphe Quetelet
figures.role: Applied the curve to human populations (1835)

stories.hook: In 1809, Carl Friedrich Gauss needed to tame astronomical errors — and found the curve that rules statistics.
stories.narrative: Gauss was trying to predict the orbit of Ceres from messy observations, and every measurement disagreed slightly. His solution, published in the 'Theoria motus' of 1809, was to model errors as following a particular bell-shaped curve — the curve that made the most probable value the average, and large errors exponentially unlikely. Least squares was born, and with it the normal distribution's reign. But Gauss wasn't first to the curve: Abraham de Moivre, a French Protestant exile scraping by in London coffee houses, had derived it in 1738 as the limiting shape of coin-flip probabilities in 'The Doctrine of Chances' — the first central limit theorem, seventy years early. Pierre-Simon Laplace generalized it. Then Adolphe Quetelet, a Belgian astronomer turned social scientist, did something radical in 1835: he applied the curve to people. Measuring soldiers' heights, he found the bell curve again — and invented 'l'homme moyen,' the average man, founding quantitative social science and, not incidentally, the body mass index. Francis Galton ran with it from there. The curve's ubiquity has a deep reason — the central limit theorem says averages of many small effects are always approximately normal — which is why it appears in measurement error, biology, finance, and exam scores alike. When you meet the normal distribution in this module, remember it was found three times: in gambling mathematics, in the stars, and in the heights of soldiers. Reality keeps drawing the same bell. Quetelet's "average man" had a dark twin: the same statistics were soon used to rank human worth, a history the ethical analyst must know. The curve itself is innocent — the central limit theorem guarantees it wherever many small effects add up — but its applications never are. In this module you'll wield the normal distribution constantly; wield it knowing both its power and its past.
stories.title: The story behind the bell curve
verifiedClaims: De Moivre derived the normal curve as a limit in 1738
Gauss developed it for errors in the Theoria motus (1809)
Quetelet applied it to human measurements in 1835

stories.bridge: Euler drew the first graph to settle a bet about bridges. Now let's learn graph theory properly — the mathematics of everything connected.

figures.name: Leonhard Euler
figures.role: Founded graph theory with the Königsberg paper (1736)

stories.hook: In 1736, Leonhard Euler settled a bar bet about seven bridges — and invented a new mathematics.
stories.narrative: The Prussian city of Königsberg was built on two islands in the Pregel River, connected to each other and the banks by seven bridges, and the locals had a puzzle: could you walk a route that crossed each bridge exactly once? Euler, the great Swiss mathematician working in St. Petersburg, realized the puzzle wasn't about distances or geography at all. He stripped it down: land masses became points, bridges became lines connecting them. The question became whether a path could traverse each line exactly once. In 'Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis' (1736), he proved it impossible — a walk using every bridge once exists only if zero or two land masses have an odd number of bridges, and Königsberg had four. The paper founded two fields at once: graph theory, the mathematics of points and connections, and topology, the 'geometry of position' he named in the title. Euler himself considered it a trifle, a recreational diversion from serious analysis. The trifle ate the world: graphs now model the internet, social networks, supply chains, molecules, and proofs; the Eulerian path he characterized is the mathematics behind route inspection, DNA sequencing, and network design. When you draw your first graph in this module — vertices, edges, degrees — you're using Euler's 1736 abstraction. He reduced a city to dots and lines to win a bet. You'll reduce systems to dots and lines to understand them. Same move, bigger bridges. Euler's "trifle" now underpins the module's hardest problems: the traveling salesman on graphs, network flows, the PageRank you'll meet elsewhere in this program. The Königsberg walk is still the right first proof to learn — it teaches the move that defines the field: strip away the geography, keep the connections. Dots and lines, 1736 to today. Same move, bigger bridges — learn it well.
stories.title: The story behind graph theory
verifiedClaims: Euler's Königsberg paper was published in 1736
It characterized Eulerian paths via odd-degree vertices
The paper founded graph theory and contributed to topology
